blocks.text: El Niño-driven drought is threatening farmers in Malawi and far beyond. Credit...
Chico Harlan, Golden Matonga and Joao Silva spent four days in Namasoko, a village seven hours outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Hundreds of farmers were gathered under the village’s biggest wild mango tree, summoned by the chief, when the government workers arrived with a dire warning. Drought was soon likely to hit. The farmers had better prepare.

The cause, they said, is this year’s extraordinarily powerful El Niño, a global weather phenomenon born in the Pacific Ocean, half a world away from their village of Namasoko, Malawi, in southern Africa.
If the farmers bought special drought-resistant seeds, they might be able to avoid hunger and financial despair. But a single bag costs $43. And most farmers make less than $3 per day.
“What are we to do?” asked Patrick Hareke, 46, one of the farmers.
It’s a question being asked across the developing world.

Preparing for El Niño is daunting even in good times. The natural phenomenon scrambles global weather in ways that are both predictable and economically devastating. It typically causes droughts in Latin America and southern Africa that hit one group above all: poor farmers who are at the mercy of the skies.
